title: Reduced flat base change on alteration objects, products and generators
statement: Let $S,S'$ be reduced Noetherian schemes [def-pc-reduced-scheme, def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring], let $h:S'\to S$ be flat [def-weil-flat-morphism], and assume each fibre stays reduced after every finite extension of its residue field. Fix a prime $\ell$. Use the category $\operatorname{alt}/S$ and the two classes of generating families from [def-per-prime-to-ell-alteration-topology]. Then ordinary scheme base change $F(T)=T\times_S S'$ [def-pc-fibre-product] is an object of $\operatorname{alt}/S'$ for every object $T$ of $\operatorname{alt}/S$, and gives a functor on their morphisms. This functor preserves the terminal object and categorical fibre products: the image of any universal fibre-product cone in $\operatorname{alt}/S$ is a universal fibre-product cone in $\operatorname{alt}/S'$. The categorical fibre product here is the reduced union of the irreducible components of the ordinary product that dominate components of the base, rather than in general the whole ordinary product. Moreover $F$ sends every $\ell'$-decomposed etale generating family to a $\ell'$-decomposed etale family, and every proper surjective maximally $\ell'$-finite generating morphism to a proper surjective maximally $\ell'$-finite morphism. These assertions concern the generators, without assuming regularity of $T$ or asserting a normal crossings conclusion.

source.place: Expose II 1.1.5, 1.2.3 fourth bullet, 1.2.5--1.2.8, 2.1.1 and the generator calculation underlying 2.3.4, printed pp.23--28; flat base change of the maximal-dominant reduced part gives the asserted categorical products.

proof.text: For an object $T\to S$, finite type is preserved by ordinary base change, so $T\prime=T\times_S S\prime$ is of finite type over $S\prime$ and is Noetherian. The finite-extension hypothesis makes $h$ geometrically reduced: on each affine open $\operatorname{Spec}A$ of a fibre $h_s$, its scalar extensions for finite purely inseparable fields are reduced; the affine-spectrum and tensor-product identifications give the same assertion for $A\otimes_{\kappa(s)}L$. The existing finite-inseparable test gives reducedness for every field extension, and the affine open-cover criterion gives it for the whole fibre. Every field-valued point of $S$ factors through its residue field, so this is the hypothesis of the Mathlib reduced-pullback lemma. Apply that lemma to the reduced Noetherian $T$ to obtain reducedness of $T\prime$. Flat base change preserves maximal dominance, so every generic point of $T\prime$ maps to a generic point $s\prime$ of $S\prime$. The flat map $h$ sends $s\prime$ to a generic point $s$ of $S$. The generic-fibre criterion says $T_s$ is finite over $\kappa(s)$. Its scalar extension to $\kappa(s\prime)$ is still finite: on coordinate rings a finite spanning set tensors to a finite spanning set. Hence the residue fields of its points, in particular those of the generic points of $T\prime$, are finite over $\kappa(s\prime)$. This verifies every object condition.

An $S$-morphism $u:T\to V$ induces the unique $S\prime$-morphism $u\prime:T\times_S S\prime\to V\times_S S\prime$ with the prescribed projections. Uniqueness in the scheme fibre-product universal property shows $(vu)\prime=v\prime u\prime$ and $(1_T)\prime=1_{T\prime}$. As $S$ and $S\prime$ are reduced, their identity maps are objects and terminal in their alteration categories. The canonical scheme isomorphism $S\times_S S\prime\simeq S\prime$ therefore identifies the image of the terminal object with the terminal object.

source.place: II 1.2.2 and 1.2.3 first and fourth bullets.

proof.text: For a diagram $X\to Z\leftarrow Y$ in $\operatorname{alt}/S$, put $C=X\times_Z Y$ and $P=C_{\mathrm{md}}$. The product clause of the alteration calculus identifies $P$ as its categorical pullback. These are finite-type $S$-schemes: the morphisms of the diagram are locally of finite type by cancellation, and are quasi-compact since their sources are Noetherian (every open of a Noetherian space is quasi-compact); then apply finite-type composition and base change. Set $C\prime=C\times_S S\prime$ and $P\prime=P\times_S S\prime$. The latter is reduced by step 1, since $P$ is an alteration object. For every generic $s$ of $S$, $C_s=X_s\times_{Z_s}Y_s$ is finite: its coordinate algebra is a tensor product of finite-dimensional $\kappa(s)$-algebras over the finite-dimensional algebra of $Z_s$, hence a quotient of their tensor product over $\kappa(s)$. The base change of $P\hookrightarrow C$ is a closed immersion. By maximal-dominance stability $P\prime$ is maximally dominant over $S\prime$, so its closed support is contained in $|(C\prime)_{\mathrm{md}}|$. Conversely let $c\prime$ be a generic point of a component of $C\prime$ dominating $S\prime$. Its image $s\prime$ in $S\prime$ maps to a generic point $s$ of $S$, by flatness of $h$. Its image in $C$ therefore lies in $C_s$, whose whole support is contained in $P$ by the dominant-part statement. Thus $c\prime$ belongs to the inverse image $|P\prime|$; as this subset is closed it contains its whole component. The supports coincide. Both closed subschemes are reduced, so uniqueness of the reduced induced closed subscheme gives $P\prime\simeq(C\prime)_{\mathrm{md}}$ over $C\prime$.

source.place: II 1.2.5--1.2.6 and flat base-change component comparison (II 1.1.3, 1.1.5).

proof.text: The scheme fibre-product universal property identifies $C\prime$ canonically with $X\prime\times_{Z\prime}Y\prime$, compatibly with the two projections. Step 3 and the product clause of the alteration calculus now identify $P\prime$ with the categorical fibre product of $X\prime$ and $Y\prime$ over $Z\prime$. Any other universal cone over the original diagram has a unique isomorphism to the cone with vertex $P$; applying the functor of step 2 and this isomorphism proves the assertion for every universal cone.

Let $(U_i\to T)_i$ be an $\ell\prime$-decomposed etale generating family. Its members after base change are objects by step 1, and the induced family over $T\prime$ is etale by etale-covering base change. For $t\prime\in T\prime$ with image $t\in T$, choose $u\in U_i$ over $t$ of finite residue degree prime to $\ell$. Apply the residue-base-change lemma to $\kappa(u)/\kappa(t)$ and $K=\kappa(t\prime)$. It gives a point of $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(u)\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(t)}\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(t\prime)$ with finite residue degree prime to $\ell$ over $\kappa(t\prime)$. The field-fibre inclusion $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(u)\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(t)}\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(t\prime)\to U_i\times_T T\prime\simeq U_i\times_S S\prime$ sends this point to a point $w$ over $u$ and $t\prime$ whose attached prime of $\kappa(u)\otimes_{\kappa(t)}\kappa(t\prime)$ is the given one, and the fibre-product residue-field lemma identifies $\kappa(w)$ with its residue field, compatibly with $\kappa(t\prime)$; so $w$ has exactly that residue degree. This supplies the required lift of every $t\prime$.

Let $f:U\to T$ be a proper surjective maximally $\ell\prime$-finite generator. The map $f\prime:U\prime\to T\prime$ is proper and surjective by their ordinary base-change lemmas. Let $t\prime$ be a generic point of $T\prime$. The projection $T\prime\to T$ is flat, hence sends $t\prime$ to a generic point $t$. Choose a generic $u\in U$ over $t$ with finite residue degree prime to $\ell$. The residue-base-change lemma gives a point of $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(u)\otimes_{\kappa(t)}\kappa(t\prime)$ with finite residue degree prime to $\ell$; its image $u\prime\in U\prime$ lies over $u$ and $t\prime$, and by the fibre-product residue-field lemma $\kappa(u\prime)$ is that residue field over $\kappa(t\prime)$. It is a generic point of $U\prime$: its image $s\prime$ in $S\prime$ is generic by step 1, and the generic-fibre criterion makes $(U\prime)_{s\prime}$ finite over a field. Any generalization of $u\prime$ must lie in this fibre, since $s\prime$ has no strict generalizations; all points of a finite scheme over a field are closed and have no strict generalizations. Thus $u\prime$ has no strict generalization. Finally, for every generic point $v\prime$ of $U\prime$, its image in $T\prime$ lies over the same generic point of $S\prime$. Step 1 gives finiteness of $\kappa(v\prime)/\kappa(s\prime)$; its intermediate field $\kappa(f\prime(v\prime))$ therefore gives finiteness of $\kappa(v\prime)/\kappa(f\prime(v\prime))$. These are both clauses of maximal $\ell\prime$-finiteness.
